newsitem.title: USA: Leap second makes Monday longest day of the year.
newsitem.headline: Leap second makes Monday longest day of the year.

text.p: Monday will be the longest day of the year after timekeepers add a second to precisely synchronize atomic clocks to the spinning of the earth, a U.S. government agency said.

The adjustment is necessary because it is not possible to precisely predict how fast the earth will spin on its axis, said Collier Smith, spokesman for the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a division of the U.S. Department of Commerce. So timekeepers add a second every year or so to put the clocks in line.

Just before 8 p.m. EDT, which is midnight Greenwich Mean Time (the international time standard), a leap second was scheduled to be inserted at the Time and Frequency Division in Boulder, Colo., and at the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C. Operators of standard clocks around the world will do the same.
Adding a second is a simple procedure, Smith said. "They punch a button and it subtracts out one pulse -- just like grabbing hold of the second hand."
The adjustment is decreed by the International Earth Rotation Service in France, and Monday's was the 21st adjustment of its kind to the world's time since 1972.

The precise time is important for telephone companies, broadcasting, maritime and aviation navigation systems, computer networks, electric utilities and many other scientific applications. Telecommunication systems and others needing precise time can pick up signals from atomic clocks through satellite systems or the Internet.
The last leap second was on Dec. 31, 1995, and the last summertime leap was on June 30, 1994. Adjustments are made on the last day of either June or December.
